Jalen Brooks

gap-013 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I'm funny when I know people. Teachers say I could do better, which I already know, so hearing it again doesn't really help. I can remember everything about a game and forget one worksheet. I don't think that means I'm lazy at everything. Mostly I want people to stop asking what I'm going to be, because I don't have an answer that sounds good yet.

  • family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; nearby cousins visit most weekends.
  • finances: Stable working household with careful spending and one shared family computer.
  • geography: Garland, Texas; has lived in the same apartment complex since kindergarten.
  • cultureLanguages: Black American family; English at home; family gatherings often center on sports and food.
  • school: Large comprehensive public high school; generally attends, but completes little work in two classes.
  • accessOpportunities: School teams, neighborhood basketball courts, library, reliable phone internet, and parents who can occasionally provide rides.
  • Age 4–5

    Jalen spent preschool afternoons in his grandmother's apartment while his parents worked. He liked lining up toy cars by which ones looked fastest, then abandoned the arrangement when cousins arrived. Adults called him sociable because he followed older children everywhere. He was much quieter around unfamiliar adults and often let his cousin answer questions for him.

  • Age 6–7

    In first grade he learned to read on schedule but disliked reading aloud when classmates might laugh. Recess mattered more to him than classroom rewards. His father signed him up for basketball, and Jalen enjoyed the uniforms and postgame snacks as much as playing. At home he could spend a whole evening replaying one racing game.

  • Age 8–9

    By nine he knew which neighborhood children were good at which games and arranged teams so his friends stayed together. Teachers found him pleasant and easily distracted. He usually finished worksheets if someone sat nearby. He began asking for expensive sneakers after an older cousin explained which brands people noticed, although his parents rarely agreed to buy them.

  • Age 10–11

    During remote schooling he kept his camera off and sometimes played games after opening the required assignments. His mother discovered several missing projects late in the semester. The resulting restrictions produced arguments but did not create a lasting homework routine. Online matches became a reliable place to meet friends when visits and basketball practices were interrupted.

  • Age 12–13

    Returning to school, Jalen cared intensely about sitting with the right lunch group. He practiced basketball enough to make a school squad but disliked conditioning and eventually stopped trying out. A short relationship conducted mostly through messages ended awkwardly. He deleted photographs together but still checked the girl's posts. His grades varied according to how closely teachers monitored him.

  • Age 14–15

    He became the regular organizer of his friends' evening gaming sessions, remembering schedules and settling minor disagreements over team choices. In class, he could explain material verbally and still leave the written assignment blank. His parents argued about whether taking away his console would help. Jalen found their arguments embarrassing and avoided inviting friends over when tensions were high.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen he works one Saturday shift stocking drinks at an uncle's convenience store, a routine he finds tolerable when the store is quiet. He knows the shelves and notices missing products without prompting. He remains behind in English and chemistry. His closest friend has started making other plans, leaving Jalen unsure how much of their group will last.

Life now

  • enjoys: Competitive online basketball games · Sneaker videos · Hanging around the apartment court
  • avoids: Long written assignments · Being publicly corrected · Unfamiliar organized activities
  • activities: Evening gaming with friends · Saturday drink stocking · Occasional pickup basketball
  • demonstratedSkills: Coordinates friends across schedules · Recognizes shelf gaps · Explains familiar game strategies clearly
  • unfamiliarActivities: Laboratory work beyond required classes · Programming · Independent travel
  • motivations: Keeping his place in his friend group · Having spending money · Being seen as competent
  • ambitions: Wants a job that pays enough for his own car · Sometimes says he will keep playing competitive games; has no concrete plan
  • struggles: Persistent missing assignments · Attention divided between phone and homework · Friendship insecurity
  • supports: Parents remain involved · Uncle offers predictable paid work · Longstanding neighborhood friendships
  • practicalConstraints: Shared computer · Parents cannot drive him to activities every evening · Limited savings

Still uncertain: Will he accept structured help for the missing coursework? · How much does he enjoy games themselves versus being with the group? · What will he choose if his friends reduce their gaming time?
